prompt.context: Our client is a major provider of long-distance telephone service in the United States. It owns a subsidiary that is a communications satellite company – in the business of launching satellites and then marketing (selling or leasing) the transponders on the satellite to companies or to phone service providers. The subsidiary has proposed a $400 million expansion involving new satellites, and the client would like to know whether this is a good investment or not. The satellite subsidiary has not been making a return on capital up to the parent company's standards, and the client is not even sure if it should be in this business – they may want to sell it.
prompt.question: What do you tell them? Should the client keep the satellite subsidiary, invest $400 million in it, or sell it?

clarifying_info.q: What were the subsidiary's revenues last year?
clarifying_info.a: $50 million in revenues and $48 million in costs, for a profit before taxes of $2 million.

clarifying_info.q: Where did the $50 million in revenues come from?
clarifying_info.a: $40 million was from annual leases for 20 of the firm's 100 transponders. $10 million was from annual service charges on the 80 transponders used by customers outside the parent company, including both the 20 that are leased out and 60 transponders that were sold before the satellite was launched. 20 of the company's 100 transponders are used by the parent company and the subsidiary receives no revenue for that.

$28 million for tracking and otherwise operating the satellite, and $20 million that the parent company is charging the subsidiary each year for 5 years to cover the cost of a satellite that was destroyed upon launch a few years ago.

Satellites are a very risky business – 1 in 7 of all new satellites fail when launched – and thus satellites are frequently insured for far less than their value because insurance is very expensive. There is also a 10% chance of failure over five years for every satellite in operation.

clarifying_info.q: Is the satellite market commodified? Can the parent get transponder capacity elsewhere?
clarifying_info.a: The satellite market is fairly commodified. The parent does not need to own a satellite company to protect its usage – they could get transponder leases for the same price from any number of providers with the same quality of service, and there is no shortage expected.

framework: First determine whether to keep the subsidiary at all before considering the $400M investment
Assess true profitability by identifying hidden revenues (value of services provided to parent for free) and non-recurring costs (failed satellite write-off)
If subsidiary is worth keeping, evaluate the $400M expansion on its merits (profitability, risk, strategic fit)
If client still wants to sell, explore strategic rationale: capital needs, core competency focus, risk/return mismatch between businesses
Consider competitive and strategic implications of selling (e.g., competitor acquiring the asset, future technology shifts)

questions.prompt: Calculate the subsidiary's true economic revenues and profitability, accounting for all value flows including services provided to the parent at no charge.
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies that the 20 transponders used by the parent represent hidden revenue that would need to be paid to a third party if the subsidiary were sold. Lease value for those 20 transponders = $40M/20 * 20 = $40M. Service charge per transponder = $10M/80 = $125,000; for 20 transponders = $2.5M. Total hidden revenue = $42.5M. Adjusted revenues = $50M + $42.5M = $92.5M (the candidate in the case computed $45M of hidden value for $95M total, with a noted math error of $2.5M). True costs should exclude the $20M recurring charge for the destroyed satellite as it is a sunk cost that should have been taken as a one-time charge, not a recurring expense. Adjusted costs = $28M. Adjusted profit = ~$64–67M, making the subsidiary highly profitable.

math.setup: Hidden lease revenue for 20 parent transponders: $40M total lease / 20 leased transponders = $2M per transponder/year; 20 parent transponders * $2M = $40M. Hidden service charge: $10M / 80 transponders = $125,000 per transponder; 20 parent transponders * $125,000 = $2.5M. Total hidden revenue = $42.5M. Adjusted revenues = $50M + $42.5M = $92.5M. Non-recurring cost to exclude: $20M/year charged by parent for failed satellite (sunk cost). True operating cost = $28M.
steps: Remove non-recurring failed-satellite charge: $48M costs - $20M = $28M true annual cost
math.answer: Adjusted annual profit before tax ≈ $64.5M on $92.5M revenues; the subsidiary is highly profitable and should be kept.

questions.prompt: Given that the subsidiary is profitable and the $400M investment is assumed to be worthwhile, what factors should the client consider when deciding whether to sell the subsidiary anyway?
questions.guidance: A strong answer covers: (1) Loss of future revenue stream vs. sale proceeds; (2) Continued access to transponders at fair market price (since market is commodified); (3) Risk that a competitor acquires the subsidiary and gains a strategic asset; (4) Future technology shifts (cellular/satellite convergence) that could make ownership more valuable; (5) Capital needs of the core long-distance business; (6) Focus on core competency (like AT&T spinning off Lucent); (7) Risk/return mismatch – long-distance is steady low-risk, satellites are high-risk (1-in-7 launch failure rate, 10% in-operation failure rate), and the parent's shareholders may be too risk-averse for satellite exposure.

questions.prompt: The client has decided to sell despite the profitability analysis. What could be driving that decision?
questions.guidance: Key insight: the long-distance business has a steady, low-risk return profile while satellites have very high operational and launch risk (1 in 7 launches fail, 10% in-operation failure per 5 years). The parent's shareholders are risk-averse and the two businesses have fundamentally different risk/return profiles that are a poor match under one corporate roof. Additional factors: need for capital in core business, desire to focus on core competency, belief both companies perform better as separate entities.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should the client consider when deciding whether to sell the satellite subsidiary?

categories.name: Financial / Valuation
ideas: Loss of future high-margin revenue stream from leases and service charges
Sale proceeds vs. NPV of retaining
Whether sale price reflects the true economic value including hidden parent-usage revenues

categories.name: Strategic / Competitive
ideas: Risk of competitor acquiring the subsidiary and denying capacity or gaining strategic capability
Future technology trend toward satellite/cellular convergence could make ownership more valuable
Ability to influence satellite capacity expansion to meet growing parent demand

categories.name: Operational / Access
ideas: Parent currently uses 20 transponders at zero cost; post-sale would pay market rates
Market is commodified so replacement service is available at same price and quality
No shortage of transponder supply expected

categories.name: Corporate / Portfolio Fit
ideas: Long-distance is low-risk steady business; satellites are high-risk (launch failure, in-operation failure)
Shareholder risk tolerance may not suit satellite volatility
Focus on core competency; precedent of AT&T spinning off Lucent
Capital freed up for reinvestment in core long-distance business

recommendation: The subsidiary is highly profitable when true economic revenues (~$92.5M) and only recurring costs ($28M) are used; the parent should keep it
The $400M expansion should be evaluated on standard ROI/NPV criteria given the subsidiary's strong underlying economics

If the client still chooses to sell, the primary driver is a fundamental risk/return mismatch: long-distance is steady and low-risk while satellites carry high launch and operational risk inconsistent with shareholder risk appetite
risks: Selling at a price that undervalues hidden parent-usage revenues
Post-sale dependence on third-party satellite providers (mitigated by commodified market)
Competitor acquiring the asset and gaining future strategic leverage if satellite technology becomes critical
next_steps: Recalculate subsidiary valuation using adjusted revenues to ensure any sale price is fair
Evaluate the $400M expansion NPV including risk-adjusted failure probabilities
If selling, negotiate a long-term transponder lease agreement at favorable rates before completing the transaction
Assess whether a partial stake sale or spin-off structure could preserve strategic access while monetizing the asset
